passive_intel.description:
Scan proxy history for sensitive data: cloud and API keys (AWS, Google, GitHub including fine-grained github_pat_, GitLab glpat-, OpenAI sk-proj-, Anthropic sk-ant-, Slack, Stripe), JWTs, private keys, internal IPs and URLs, S3/Azure/GCS buckets, source-map URLs, stack traces, SQL errors, server versions and sensitive paths. Zero-effort intelligence gathering from traffic already captured: no request is sent. Binary bodies are skipped and each body is scanned up to 200000 characters. A finding is one distinct value of a category: where it was first seen (url, request or response), how many such places carry it ("occurrences") and up to 4 more of them ("also_seen"). At most 100 distinct values per category, so a token sent on every page takes one slot; further values are counted in "omitted".

Parameters: max_items (int, default 1000), in_scope_only (bool, default false), categories (optional array of pattern names; a partial name such as "aws" selects every pattern containing it), host_filter (optional regex).

Available categories: aws_access_key, aws_secret_key, google_api_key, google_oauth_token, github_token, github_fine_grained_token, gitlab_token, openai_api_key, anthropic_api_key, slack_token, stripe_key, jwt_token, bearer_token, basic_auth, private_key, email_address, ipv4_internal, phone_number, s3_bucket, azure_storage, gcs_bucket, internal_url, graphql_endpoint, api_endpoint, source_map_url, stack_trace, sql_error, server_version, framework_version, php_version, sensitive_path. email_address and phone_number match too much to be useful by default and run only when named in categories.

Returns the endpoints, each with the security requirement it is under, and security_schemes, which says how every credential is carried. tools.name: auth_diff
tools.description:
Authorization level diffing: sends the same request with different auth levels (admin, user, unauthenticated) and compares responses to detect IDOR, privilege escalation, and broken access control.

Provide auth_levels as an array of at least 2 objects: [{"name": "admin", "header_name": "Authorization", "header_value": "Bearer admin-token"}, {"name": "user", "header_name": "Authorization", "header_value": "Bearer user-token"}, {"name": "none"}]. A level that needs several headers (session cookie + CSRF token) lists them in "headers": {"Cookie": "...", "X-CSRF-Token": "..."}; "remove_headers": ["X-Tenant-Key"] drops headers for that level.

A level's headers replace the request's own (never a second Cookie/Authorization line). A level named "none"/"unauth"/"anonymous" is sent without credentials: Authorization, Cookie, API-key/token headers and every header another level uses for its identity are stripped. Content-Length is corrected for every level. Each response reports headers_set / headers_removed / credential_headers_kept so you can check what was sent.

Analyzes status codes, body content, body length, and headers for differences. Flags critical findings like identical responses across auth levels — except when the target looks like a static asset (content-type or file extension: CSS/JS/image/font), where identical-across-levels is expected and the finding is downgraded to informational instead. Levels that are all refused alike (same 401/403/404/5xx, a redirect to a login page, or a 200 that only carries a login page or a denial message) are informational, never high or critical. A level that times out is listed under errors and not compared.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check.

tools.name: bambda_import
tools.description: Import a Bambda into Burp Suite. A real .bambda file is a YAML-ish envelope — id, name, function, location, then a 'source:' block holding the Java-like lambda body — not a bare lambda expression. 'script' may be that envelope (header keys at the start of a line, in any order, comments allowed), or just the bare lambda body, which is wrapped using 'name'/'function'/'location' (or sensible defaults) and a generated id. An envelope missing id, name, function or location gets them the same way. The result carries the Bambda's 'id'; importing that id again replaces it. Use bambda_templates for the format, the known functions and locations, and starting points.

tools.description: Get the .bambda envelope format, the function types and locations known from PortSwigger's public Bambda repository (with what each one receives and must return), and a starting lambda body for each kind: proxy, WebSocket, Logger and site map filters, a custom column, match and replace, a Repeater custom action, and passive and active scan checks. Pass a template's 'source' to bambda_import as 'script' with its name, function and location. No parameters required.

tools.name: collaborator
tools.description:
Burp Collaborator out-of-band testing: clients, payloads, polling.
Call one action as collaborator.<action> (MCP clients put the action in the "action" parameter); * marks a required parameter. Example: {"do":"collaborator.restore_client"}
- collaborator.create_client(): Create a Burp Collaborator client for out-of-band (OOB) payloads; its secret key is saved in the Burp project, so it survives an extension reload.
- collaborator.restore_client(secret_key*): Restore a Collaborator client from its secret key (clients created in this Burp project come back by themselves; this is for a key from elsewhere).
- collaborator.get_secret(client_id*): Get the secret key for a Collaborator client.
- collaborator.generate_payload(client_id*, custom_data): Generate a unique Collaborator payload (subdomain) for OOB detection and return its payload_id, the id carried by every interaction it causes.
- collaborator.default_payload(without_server_location): Generate a Collaborator payload using Burp's DEFAULT generator (no client_id needed).
- collaborator.poll(client_id*, type, payload_id, since, limit, max_body_length): Poll for Collaborator interactions (DNS, HTTP with full request and response, SMTP); all are kept in a history, so filters and repeated polls lose nothing.
- collaborator.server_info(client_id*): Get the Collaborator server address and metadata for a given client.
- collaborator.remove_client(client_id*): Drop a Collaborator client from Raijin's tracking, with its saved secret key and its recorded interactions, so it is not restored on the next load.
- collaborator.list_clients(): List the Collaborator clients registered in this Burp project, including the ones restored after an extension reload.

client_id.description: Collaborator client id [actions: get_secret, generate_payload, poll, server_info, remove_client]

custom_data.description: Custom data to embed in the payload, echoed back by its interactions (up to 16 alphanumeric characters) [actions: generate_payload]

without_server_location.description: Omit the server location from the payload (default false) [actions: default_payload]

payload_id.description: Return only interactions of this payload: the payload_id from collaborator.generate_payload, or the payload host [actions: poll]

since.description: Return only interactions after this cursor: the next_since of an earlier poll, or a seq. Without it a poll returns the whole history again [actions: poll]

limit.description: Maximum interactions to return, oldest first (default 100); has_more means more follow, continue from next_since [actions: poll]

max_body_length.description: Truncate each HTTP body and SMTP conversation at N characters (default 200000) [actions: poll]

create_client.description: Create a Burp Collaborator client for out-of-band (OOB) payloads; its secret key is saved in the Burp project, so it survives an extension reload. Returns a client ID and the Collaborator server address; collaborator.list_clients shows what is registered. Pro edition only.

restore_client.description: Restore a Collaborator client from its secret key (clients created in this Burp project come back by themselves; this is for a key from elsewhere). That covers a client from another project and one dropped with collaborator.remove_client. A key that is already registered returns its existing client. Pro edition only.

get_secret.description: Get the secret key for a Collaborator client. Within this Burp project the client is restored automatically; keep the key to bring the client back elsewhere, or after collaborator.remove_client, with collaborator.restore_client.

generate_payload.description: Generate a unique Collaborator payload (subdomain) for OOB detection and return its payload_id, the id carried by every interaction it causes. Use this payload in injection points to detect blind vulnerabilities (SSRF, blind XSS, etc.), then pass payload_id to collaborator.poll to see only this payload's interactions. Optionally embed custom data in the payload for identification.

custom_data.description: Custom data to embed in the payload, echoed back by its interactions (up to 16 alphanumeric characters)

default_payload.description: Generate a Collaborator payload using Burp's DEFAULT generator (no client_id needed). Unlike collaborator.generate_payload, these payloads are linked to Burp's NATIVE Collaborator tab — interactions show up there but CANNOT be polled via collaborator.poll. Use when you want hits visible in Burp's own Collaborator UI rather than via API polling.

without_server_location.description: Omit the server location from the payload (default false)

poll.description: Poll for Collaborator interactions (DNS, HTTP with full request and response, SMTP); all are kept in a history, so filters and repeated polls lose nothing. Results are read from that bounded history: type and payload_id only narrow what is returned (filtered_out counts the interactions they left out), and polling again returns the same interactions plus new ones. Pass since=<next_since of the previous result> to get only newer ones. Each interaction has seq, payload_id (as returned by collaborator.generate_payload), client address, timestamp and details: the DNS query type, name and raw hex (query_name_error when the query does not decode), the HTTP request and response (headers and bodies), or the SMTP conversation. has_more means limit cut the page (continue from next_since); history_truncated means older interactions were dropped from the history.

payload_id.description: Return only interactions of this payload: the payload_id from collaborator.generate_payload, or the payload host

since.description: Return only interactions after this cursor: the next_since of an earlier poll, or a seq. Without it a poll returns the whole history again

limit.description: Maximum interactions to return, oldest first (default 100); has_more means more follow, continue from next_since

max_body_length.description: Truncate each HTTP body and SMTP conversation at N characters (default 200000)

server_info.description: Get the Collaborator server address and metadata for a given client.

remove_client.description: Drop a Collaborator client from Raijin's tracking, with its saved secret key and its recorded interactions, so it is not restored on the next load. Montoya's Collaborator API has no server-side client teardown (a client is just a secret-key handle, not a resource Burp needs told to close) — this is local bookkeeping only. list_clients.description: List the Collaborator clients registered in this Burp project, including the ones restored after an extension reload. Per client: client_id, server, created_at, restored, persisted (secret key saved in the project), payloads_generated and interactions_recorded (what collaborator.poll has fetched so far; this tool does not contact the Collaborator server). A saved client that Burp could not restore is listed under 'unrestored' with the reason.

bcheck_create.description: Generate and deploy a BCheck custom scan check from structured parameters. BChecks are Burp Suite's DSL for defining custom vulnerability detection rules that run during scanning. Any text is safe in any parameter: it is written into the script as a string, never as DSL. Parameters: name (required, check name), description (required, what it detects), type (required), severity (required), confidence (required), author (optional, defaults to Raijin AI Agent), tags (optional, comma-separated), issue_detail, issue_remediation, and the definition: passive_response: match_pattern is looked for in match_location (response_body, the default; response_headers; status_code). passive_request: match_pattern is looked for in match_location (request_url, the default; request_headers; request_body). insertion_point: each of payloads is injected, and the check reports when response_match_pattern appears in the response body and was not in the response to the unmodified request. host_level: one GET of path (default /) per host, reported when the answer is 200 and its body shows response_match_pattern. path_level: each of payloads is a suffix appended to every path (default .bak, .old, .orig, .swp, ~), reported when the answer is 200, differs from the answer to a random path and, if given, shows response_match_pattern. collaborator: the header named by match_location (default Referer) is set to match_pattern, which must contain {generate_collaborator_address()} (default https://{generate_collaborator_address()}); reported on a collaborator_payload_type (dns, the default, or http) interaction. match_condition says how a pattern is compared: matches (regex, the default), contains (literal substring) or is (exact value); comparisons are case-sensitive unless a regex says (?i). An empty or missing pattern is rejected, since it would match everything. Use custom_check.bcheck_dry_run with the same definition to see what it does with the recorded proxy history first, and custom_check.bcheck_templates for the DSL itself.

The script must include a metadata block with language, name, and description fields, followed by the check logic. Parameters: script (required, the full BCheck DSL script as a string). Use custom_check.bcheck_templates to see the correct syntax and available DSL constructs.

Note: this removes the BCheck from MCP tracking; to fully remove it from Burp Suite, manual removal in the Burp UI may be needed. Parameters: id (required, the BCheck ID from custom_check.bcheck_create or custom_check.bcheck_import).

bcheck_templates.description: Get all BCheck templates with full examples, DSL reference, and usage guidance. Returns 7 templates covering all BCheck types: passive_response, passive_request, insertion_point, host_level, path_level, collaborator, and multi_step. Each template includes a complete working example, use cases, and descriptions. Also returns a comprehensive DSL reference covering metadata fields, scope keywords, request operations, conditions, strings and escaping, variables, and reporting options. Call this BEFORE writing a BCheck script by hand. No parameters required.

bcheck_dry_run.description: Try a custom_check.bcheck_create definition against the proxy history Burp has already recorded, before deploying it. Nothing is imported and nothing is sent. A passive check is evaluated in full: the result lists the recorded messages it would report, with an excerpt of what matched. A check that sends requests cannot be run dry, so the result says how many requests a scan would add and what the history already shows: responses that carry the response pattern before any payload (insertion_point), or recorded responses for the very paths the check would request (host_level, path_level). The generated script is returned too. The definition parameters are those of custom_check.bcheck_create: passive_response: match_pattern is looked for in match_location (response_body, the default; response_headers; status_code). passive_request: match_pattern is looked for in match_location (request_url, the default; request_headers; request_body). insertion_point: each of payloads is injected, and the check reports when response_match_pattern appears in the response body and was not in the response to the unmodified request. host_level: one GET of path (default /) per host, reported when the answer is 200 and its body shows response_match_pattern. path_level: each of payloads is a suffix appended to every path (default .bak, .old, .orig, .swp, ~), reported when the answer is 200, differs from the answer to a random path and, if given, shows response_match_pattern. collaborator: the header named by match_location (default Referer) is set to match_pattern, which must contain {generate_collaborator_address()} (default https://{generate_collaborator_address()}); reported on a collaborator_payload_type (dns, the default, or http) interaction. match_condition says how a pattern is compared: matches (regex, the default), contains (literal substring) or is (exact value); comparisons are case-sensitive unless a regex says (?i). History selection: url_pattern (regex on the URL), in_scope_only, max_items (newest history items to read, default 200), max_matches (matches listed in full, default 20).

scancheck_create_passive.description: Create a passive Script-mode scan check that analyzes every response during scanning. More powerful than BCheck -- supports several conditions joined by AND or OR, negation, and regex/contains/equals matching across response body, headers, status code, request fields, and more. Parameters: name (required, check name; creating a name again replaces that check), description (required, what it detects), conditions (required, array of condition objects -- each with: location [response_body, response_headers, status_code, response_length, request_body, request_headers, request_url], pattern [regex or string], condition_type [matches (default), contains, equals; all case-insensitive], negate [true/false]), match_mode (all = every condition must hold, the default; any = one is enough), severity (required: high, medium, low, information), confidence (required: certain, firm, tentative), issue_detail (required, detailed issue description), issue_remediation (optional, how to fix). Use custom_check.scancheck_templates first to see examples and the full condition reference, and custom_check.scancheck_dry_run to see what the conditions match in the proxy history before deploying.

scancheck_create_active.description: Create an active Script-mode scan check that injects payloads at insertion points during active scanning. The check reports only when a step matches and the response to the unmodified request would not have matched the same conditions, so a pattern the page shows anyway never raises an issue. Parameters: name (required, check name; creating a name again replaces that check), description (required, what it detects), steps (required, array of step objects -- each with: payload [string to inject], response_conditions [array of condition objects like passive checks; at least one step needs a condition on the response], match_mode [all | any for that step], stop_if_no_match [boolean, default true = required step: no match or no response ends the check without a report; false = optional step]), match_mode (default for steps: all | any), severity (required: high, medium, low, information), confidence (required: certain, firm, tentative), issue_detail (required, detailed issue description), issue_remediation (optional, how to fix). Use custom_check.scancheck_templates first to see multi-step examples.

tools.name: http_fuzz
tools.description:
Fuzz an HTTP request like Burp Intruder: payloads placed at injection points, sent through Burp, every response clustered.

Injection points (first that applies):
1. Marker pairs: wrap values with § (or a custom marker): GET /api?id=§1§&name=§test§ HTTP/1.1\r\n... Each §value§ pair is a position; a position not being fuzzed keeps its value without the markers. An odd number of markers is rejected. Takes precedence over the FUZZ keyword when both appear.
2. FUZZ keyword: used only when there are no § marker pairs. Every FUZZ is an injection point. Example: GET /api?id=FUZZ HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: target.com\r\n\r\n
3. positions: non-overlapping [start, end) offsets into the request string as given.

attack_mode (Intruder's attack types):
- sniper (default): one payload set; each position in turn takes every payload, the others keep their value (with FUZZ, every occurrence takes the payload at once).
- battering_ram: one payload set; every position takes the same payload.
- pitchfork: one set per position, walked in step (request n = n-th payload of every set; as many requests as the smallest set).
- cluster_bomb: one set per position, every combination (position 1 turns fastest).
Payload sets: payloads (+ payload_library) form one set; for pitchfork/cluster_bomb give payload_sets instead (set i -> position i; with fewer sets than positions the last set is reused). encoders (e.g. ["url"], ["base64","url"]) run on each payload before it is placed: url, url_all, double_url, json, base64, base64url, html, hex, raw.

Use \r\n line endings (bare LF in the request line and headers is converted; the body is sent as typed). Content-Length is recomputed after each substitution, counted in the bytes sent (left alone with Transfer-Encoding or several Content-Length headers, for the whole run when an injection point sits on the Content-Length line, and with auto_fix_content_length=false); a request goes out as ISO-8859-1 (one byte per char), or as UTF-8 when it holds a char above U+00FF. concurrency (1-50, default 1) requests in flight, rate_limit requests/second (0 = unlimited). timeout_ms bounds each request; a failed or timed-out request is reported in its entry and the run goes on. stop_on_match ({status_codes: [int], body_regex: string}) stops after the first matching response (stopped_early:true). max_requests caps the run (default 10000).

Every response is clustered (summary: same status and bodies at least cluster_similarity % alike, default 90; timing outliers). Filters only shorten the list (hidden responses still count in the summary): hide_status [int], filter_length [int or "min-max"] (body bytes), grep_regex (keep only matches), hide_regex. report: "all" (default, every kept exchange in full), "clusters" (one line per kept request plus one full exchange per cluster), "summary" (summary only). With report=all and no max_response_length, each listed body is capped at 20000 chars. Out-of-range numbers are clamped and reported in notes.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check. The URL checked is the first planned request's.

tools.name: http_race
tools.description:
Race condition tester (TOCTOU, double-spend, limit bypass): releases N requests at once behind a real synchronisation barrier, then clusters the responses.

sync:
- "single_packet" (default): the HTTP/2 single-packet attack through Burp's synchronised parallel sender (the engine behind Repeater's "send group in parallel" and Turbo's gated Engine.BURP2): the final frames of every request leave in one TCP packet, so network jitter cannot separate them. Needs a target that speaks HTTP/2 (http_mode HTTP_2_IGNORE_ALPN forces it without ALPN). Exchanges go through Burp (site map, session rules).
- "last_byte": HTTP/1.1 last-byte synchronisation on Raijin's own connections: each request on its own connection, written except its final byte; once every connection is primed (the barrier) the final bytes go out back to back. Reports per request ttfb_ms/ttlb_ms from its release and the release spread. Bypasses Burp (no session rules, not in the site map); sni sets the TLS server name. At most 256 connections. Chosen by default when http_mode is HTTP_1.

Use the FUZZ keyword with 'payloads' for one request per payload (payloads wins over 'count'); Content-Length is recomputed after substitution in the bytes sent (auto_fix_content_length=false sends it as written); a request goes out as ISO-8859-1, or as UTF-8 when it holds a char above U+00FF. timeout_ms bounds the whole batch.

analysis: responses clustered by status code and body similarity (cluster_similarity %, default 90) with timing outliers. race_condition_likely is true when identical requests were answered in more than one way; with payloads compare the clusters with the payloads instead. An equivalent set of responses does not rule a race out: check the application state too. Out-of-range numbers are clamped and reported in notes.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check.

http_mode.description: HTTP_1 selects last_byte; HTTP_2_IGNORE_ALPN forces HTTP/2 without ALPN

timeout_ms.description: Hard timeout for the whole batch in milliseconds (0 = no hard timeout, max 600000, default 25000)

tools.name: http_send_pipeline
tools.description:
Send multiple raw HTTP/1.1 requests over ONE socket connection and read back multiple responses in order. Unlike every other http_* tool (which goes through Burp's Montoya API, strictly one request in / one response out), this opens its own raw socket — needed for HTTP desync / request-smuggling research (0.CL, stage1+stage2 probes) where a server may respond to one request with two responses, or where you need to observe exactly what came back before a connection died.

HTTP/1.1 only — http_mode must be omitted or "HTTP_1". HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and kettled H2-smuggling escape fields are Turbo-only: use turbo_run.start with Engine.HTTP2 / Engine.HTTP3 / kettled=True for those.

Never auto-fixes Content-Length — a deliberately wrong declared length is the point of this tool. If you want byte-exact control without a wrong Content-Length tripping you up, compute it yourself.

Responses are read while the requests are still being written, so a response that starts before its request is fully sent (during a pause, or between writes) is caught and timed. Response framing is strict: a negative, non-numeric or conflicting Content-Length, a bad chunk size, or chunk data without its CRLF stops reading with close_reason "error" and the reason in error, instead of guessing. Chunked trailers are read up to their blank line and returned per response.

Parameters:
- host, port (1-65535), use_tls/tls/https (alias): target. use_tls defaults to true when port is 443.
- sni (string): TLS server name to send instead of the default (host); "" sends none. Ignored without TLS.
- requests (array, required): each item has raw_request (literal \r\n escapes are decoded only when the text has no real line break) or raw_request_hex (hex-encoded bytes), same convention as http_send_raw_bytes, and optionally pauses (as in Turbo):
  - pause_before (int): n > 0 sends the first n-1 bytes, then pauses; n < 0 holds the last |n| bytes back for the pause. Clamped into the request.
  - pause_markers (array of strings): pause after every occurrence of each string in the request bytes (same \r\n escape convention as raw_request).
  - pause_ms (0-60000, default 1000): length of each pause. A pause ends early as soon as response bytes arrive, or when the server closes the connection.
- write_mode: "concat" (default; all requests written in one burst, split only at pauses) or "single_write" (one write+flush per request, with write_pause_ms between them).
- max_responses (int, 1-1000): how many responses to read before stopping (default: number of requests sent — but a 0.CL probe may produce MORE responses than requests, or fewer; set this explicitly for that case).
- idle_timeout_ms (default 2000): stop when no bytes arrive for this long after the last request byte was written.
- total_timeout_ms (default 15000): hard cap for the whole call (connect, write and read).
- keep_open (bool, default false): keep the socket open after this call so a LATER http_send_pipeline call can reuse it via connection_id. Only honored when every requested response framed cleanly, every request byte was written, and the server keeps the connection (no Connection: close, close-delimited body, or HTTP/1.0 response without keep-alive) — anything else closes the socket. Bytes received past the last returned response are handed to the next call.
- connection_id (string): reuse a socket kept open by a prior keep_open=true call. It is reused only for the same host, port, TLS and sni; otherwise it is closed, a fresh connection is opened and connection_id_target_mismatch:true is reported. This registry is separate from Montoya's own connection_id on http_send_request — different transport layers, not interchangeable. If the id is unknown (closed, evicted after 120s idle, or never existed) a fresh connection is opened and connection_reused:false is reported, rather than erroring. http_state.pipeline_connections lists and closes kept connections.
- max_response_length (int): truncate each response body in the result.
- decode_content (bool, default false): show each body with its Content-Encoding (gzip, x-gzip, deflate, br; several undone last to first) undone. br is decoded only where a bounded, streaming decoder backs it; until then it reports decode_error instead of risking an unbounded decompression.
- raw_hex_max_bytes (int, 0-10000000, default 65536): cap on each raw hex dump; 0 leaves them out.

Out-of-range numbers are clamped into range and reported in notes.

Returns:
- responses: array of {index, status_line, status_code, headers, body, framing, trailers, warnings, raw_response_hex, raw_response_bytes, raw_response_truncated, first_byte_ms, last_byte_ms, ttfb_ms, ttlb_ms, decoded_codings, decode_error}. raw_response_hex is the bytes exactly as received: any 1xx before the response, status line, headers, body with its chunk framing and trailers. body is UTF-8 text when the bytes are valid UTF-8, else one char per byte. first_byte_ms/last_byte_ms: when its first/last byte arrived. ttfb_ms/ttlb_ms: the same, counted from when the request with the same index was completely written; negative means the response started before that request was fully sent (a desync signal); absent when no request with that index was completely written. decoded_codings/decode_error: what decode_content undid, and why it stopped short.
- requests: per request {index, bytes, bytes_written, write_start_ms, write_end_ms, pauses: [{offset, at_ms, duration_ms, ended_by: "pause_ms"|"data"|"connection_closed"|"stopped"}]}.
- partial_response: {index, raw_response_hex, raw_response_bytes, raw_response_truncated, first_byte_ms, last_byte_ms} — the bytes of the unfinished response when reading stopped on fin, rst, idle, total_timeout or error.
- unparsed: {bytes, raw_hex, raw_truncated, kept_for_next_call} — bytes received past the last returned response.
- write_error: why not every request byte was written (e.g. the server closed the connection early); the responses read are still returned.
- connection_id, connection_reused, bytes_sent, bytes_received, responses_received, close_reason ("max_responses"|"idle"|"total_timeout"|"fin"|"rst"|"error"|"switching_protocols"), connection_open.
All *_ms are milliseconds with microsecond precision, counted from the first request byte written unless stated otherwise.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check. The URL checked is the first request's.

tools.name: http_send_raw_bytes
tools.description: Send a raw byte-level HTTP request for HTTP request smuggling and CRLF injection testing. Accepts either hex-encoded bytes (raw_request_hex; whitespace between digits is ignored) or request text (raw_request). Preserves exact byte sequences without normalization: raw_request's literal \r\n / \n escapes are decoded only when the text contains no real line break, and a character above U+00FF sends the whole text as UTF-8 (use raw_request_hex for exact bytes). Requires host, port, and use_tls parameters. Sends ONE request and reads ONE response (Montoya's api.http().sendRequest has no partial-read API, so a failed/timed-out send cannot report bytes_received or distinguish fin/rst — it only returns is_timeout and close_reason="timeout"|"error"). HTTP/2/3 and kettled H2-smuggling escape fields (^~, ^xNN, ...) are not available here — this is HTTP/1 only; for those, or for sending several requests over one socket and reading back several responses, use http_send_pipeline (HTTP/1.1 pipelining) or Turbo (turbo_run.start with Engine.HTTP2/HTTP3, kettled=True). Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check.

raw_request.description: Request text; literal \r\n escapes are decoded only when it has no real line breaks

timeout_ms.description: Hard timeout in milliseconds (0 = no hard timeout, max 600000, default 25000)

tools.name: http_send_request
tools.description:
Send an HTTP request through Burp Suite. Build from URL + method + headers + body, from a raw HTTP request string, or as a native HTTP/2 request with full control of its header list (pseudo-headers included). Supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, connection reuse and Burp's request options.

Parameters:
- url (string): target URL (use this OR raw_request)
- method (string): HTTP method (default GET)
- headers (object): map of header name → value. Caller-supplied headers are preserved byte-exact (Burp's default User-Agent/Accept etc. are NOT injected when headers are provided).
- body (string OR object/array): request body. If object/array, it is serialized to compact JSON automatically.
- raw_request (string): raw HTTP request text. When supplied without explicit port/use_tls, defaults to TLS:443 (modern web default). Bare LF line endings in the request line and headers become CRLF; the body is sent as typed. Content-Length is auto-recomputed if it does not match body bytes.
- http2_headers (array of {name, value} or [name, value]): a native HTTP/2 request whose header list is sent as given, pseudo-headers included (":method", ":path", ":authority", ":scheme"): repeat, reorder, omit or malform them; CR/LF and uppercase names reach the wire. When the list has no pseudo-header, the four are derived from url/method and put first. Use with url (or host/port/use_tls) and body, not with raw_request or headers; sent with http_mode HTTP_2 (default) or HTTP_2_IGNORE_ALPN. No Content-Length is added: include a "content-length" field to send one.
- host, port (int, 1-65535), use_tls (bool): explicit service overrides
- http_mode (string): "AUTO" | "HTTP_1" | "HTTP_2" | "HTTP_2_IGNORE_ALPN". HTTP/3 is not available here or anywhere through Montoya — use Turbo (turbo_run.start with Engine.HTTP3) for HTTP/3.
- connection_id (string): pins/reuses one Montoya connection, but the request still fully completes (response received) before this call returns — no pipelining. For multi-request-per-socket pipelining use http_send_pipeline.
- follow_redirects (string): "never" | "always" | "same_host" | "in_scope" — Burp follows redirects and returns the final exchange (default: Burp's default, which does not follow).
- sni (string): TLS server name to send instead of the host.
- response_timeout_ms (int, 0 = none): Burp's own timeout for reading the response; on expiry Burp gives up and has_response is false.
- verify_tls (bool, default false): make Burp verify the target's TLS certificate.
- max_response_length (int): truncate response body in result
- timeout_ms (number, 0 = no hard timeout, max 600000, default 25000): hard timeout. Returns is_timeout=true and close_reason="timeout" on expiry. Montoya has no partial-read API, so a failed/timed-out send cannot report bytes_received or distinguish fin/rst — use http_send_pipeline when that detail matters.
- preserve_headers (bool, default true): when false, falls back to Burp's httpRequestFromUrl which adds default headers
- auto_fix_content_length (bool, default true): when false, uses raw_request CL as-is. When true and the declared Content-Length didn't match the body, the result includes content_length_rewritten:{from,to}.

Out-of-range numbers are clamped and reported in notes. Returns full response with headers, body, status code, and timing; reauthenticated:<macro> when a session login macro re-established the session and sent the request again.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check. A followed redirect that lands outside scope is flagged (scope_warning), never blocked.

tools.name: http_send_request_chain
tools.description: Send a chain of HTTP requests sequentially with variable extraction between steps. Each step can extract values from its response with a regex (first capture group), a JSONPath or an XPath, and inject them into later steps via {{variable}} placeholders. Useful for CSRF tokens, session tokens, and multi-step workflows. A step's extract rules are checked before its request is sent; timeout_ms bounds each step. Optional connection_id pins/reuses one Montoya connection across every step — steps stay fully sequential either way (no pipelining); for genuine multi-request-per-socket pipelining use http_send_pipeline instead. A step reports extract_missed (rules that matched nothing) and unresolved_placeholders ({{x}} left after substitution); success needs a response. Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check. Checked per step.

'extract' MUST be an ARRAY of {name, pattern | json_path | xpath, from} objects (from = "body" (default) or "header"; a header rule takes a pattern over the 'Name: value' lines, every Set-Cookie included), e.g. extract:[{"name":"csrf","pattern":"name=csrf value=([^ ]+)"},{"name":"jwt","json_path":"$.data.token"}]. tools.name: http_send_requests_parallel
tools.description:
Send multiple HTTP requests in parallel through Burp Suite. Each request in the array can specify url, method, headers, body (string or object), or raw_request.

Mixed hosts are supported: requests are grouped by HTTP service (host+port+tls) and dispatched per-group, then merged back into the original input order. Per-group dispatch failures do not abort the batch — failed slots come back with error/phase fields.

Parameters:
- requests (array, required): per-request objects with url, method, headers, body, raw_request, host, port, use_tls, auto_fix_content_length and preserve_headers (both default true). http2_headers, follow_redirects, sni, verify_tls and response_timeout_ms are http_send_request only: an item carrying one fails to build. Each item reports its own content_length_rewritten, headers_warning and warnings (raw CR/LF removed). A group that times out or fails marks only its own items; groups not started before timeout_ms ran out come back not_sent.
- http_mode (string): "AUTO" | "HTTP_1" | "HTTP_2" | "HTTP_2_IGNORE_ALPN"
- max_response_length (int): truncate response bodies
- timeout_ms (number, 0 = no hard timeout, max 600000, default 25000): hard timeout for the entire batch

Returns array of results in original order, plus group_timings_ms and groups_dispatched.

Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check. Checked per item: a refused item carries out_of_scope and is not sent, the others go out.

cors.description: Probe a URL's CORS policy by sending crafted Origin headers and classifying the Access-Control-Allow-Origin/-Credentials response (compared trimmed, case-insensitively). Besides an unrelated origin and 'null', it sends origins built from the target's own host to catch allowlist mistakes: <host>.<other domain> (prefix match), <junk><domain> (suffix match), a dot replaced by a letter (unescaped regex dot), <host>_.<other domain>, a made-up subdomain, and the http:// origin. Each origin is sent as a GET and as an OPTIONS preflight (asking for PUT and a custom header), and a response whose ACAO follows the Origin without 'Vary: Origin' is flagged. Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check.

cache.description: Probe a URL for web cache poisoning and web cache deception. First reads the cache from the response headers (X-Cache, CF-Cache-Status, Age, Cache-Status, ...: hit / miss / not stored, and the CDN). Poisoning: sends headers and cookies a cache often leaves out of its key (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, X-Original-URL, method overrides, cookies the target sets, ...), each under a cache-buster query value used for nothing else, then asks for the same URL without the input and without a session. Status/redirect/path probes wait until cache-buster isolation is demonstrated. Unproven isolation or a changed visitor baseline gives an inconclusive verdict, not confirmation. Stops can report rate_limited, baseline_changed or cache_buster_ignored. A unique query value cannot guarantee isolation when the cache key is unknown. Deception: requests path variants the origin may treat as the page and the cache as a static file (/page/x.css, /page;x.css, /page%23x.css, ...) as the user, then without a session. Pass the logged-in user's request headers as 'headers' to prove a private page gets stored. Scope: checked against Burp's target scope per the operator's mcp_scope_mode: warn (default) sends and adds scope_warning; enforce refuses (out_of_scope=true, nothing sent); off skips the check.

injection.description: Guided injection detection with confirmation oracles (not blind fuzzing). Mark the injection point with the FUZZ keyword anywhere in the raw request: the request line, a header line such as 'Cookie: TrackingId=FUZZ', or the body. Each payload is written in the encoding that position needs (URL path/query, form body, JSON string or value, XML, cookie, header) and Content-Length is recomputed; 'encoding' overrides this. Classes: sqli (error, time, boolean), nosqli (error, server-side JavaScript boolean, operator injection, time), cmdi (command output, time, out-of-band), ssti (expression evaluation), lfi (file read), xxe (external entity, XInclude, out-of-band), ssrf (internal content in the response, out-of-band), xss (reflection context and which characters survive), open_redirect, crlf (response header injection). Out-of-band checks use a Burp Collaborator client and are skipped with a reason when Burp has none (Community Edition); an interaction that arrives after the call returned is reported by the next call. A finding needs a response that differs from the baseline (the same request with 'base_value' at FUZZ) in a way the payload explains: a timeout is never evidence, a delay must repeat while a zero-delay control stays fast, a TRUE/FALSE difference must hold over three rounds. Boolean and operator checks only narrow the query: base_value must match a real row or document. Every finding carries its payload, a confidence (certain, firm, tentative) and the evidence (baseline next to probe) to re-check it. All classes together send about 130 requests when nothing is found; pass 'classes' to narrow. Give a raw request that identity A makes to A's own object, plus 'identities' where each low-priv account declares its own 'object_id' (a resource it owns) and 'canary' (a string that appears only in its own data). For every (reader, owner) pair the tool swaps the object id to the owner's resource, replays under the reader's auth, and asserts the owner's canary appears in the reader's response — a CONFIRMED cross-user read — while filtering the own-data-reflection false positive. It also runs the identity-diff (vertical/unauth) with the id held constant, and can enumerate the id-transformation set (encodings, neighbours, type-juggling); a transformed id is only reported when the response is not the reader's own view or a not-found answer, and confirmed when another identity's canary appears in it. The id is swapped at its parameter boundary only (one path segment, one query/form/cookie/header value, one JSON value), so /v1/users/1 never becomes /v2/users/2, and Content-Length is corrected. Auto-detects the object id in path/query/body/header/cookie (preferring an identity's own object_id when the request holds it), or pin it with id_value/id_location/id_name. Bounded. - websocket.history_search(pattern*, direction, max_results, websocket_id, url, start_index): Search WebSocket proxy history using a regex pattern on message payloads.

create.description: Create a new WebSocket connection to a target URL. Constructs an HTTP upgrade request and establishes a WebSocket connection through Burp. All messages are automatically captured and available via websocket.get_messages. Parameters: url (WebSocket URL, e.g. 'wss://example.com/ws', required), headers (optional object of additional HTTP headers as key-value pairs), subprotocol (optional string, WebSocket subprotocol to request). The upgrade goes out exactly as given: a raw CR/LF in the path, query or a header is sent as written and reported in warnings. Scope: advisory only. An out-of-scope target gets scope_warning under mcp_scope_mode warn and enforce; it is never blocked.

headers.description: Additional HTTP headers as key-value pairs

send_text.description: Send a text message on an existing WebSocket connection. The message is tracked and can be retrieved later via websocket.get_messages. Parameters: connection_id (string, the WebSocket connection ID, required), message (string, the text message to send, required).

send_binary.description: Send a binary message on an existing WebSocket connection. The data is base64 (standard or URL-safe alphabet, padding optional, whitespace ignored) and is decoded before transmission; the frame is recorded as the canonical base64 of the bytes sent. Parameters: connection_id (string, the WebSocket connection ID, required), data (string, base64-encoded binary data to send, required).

close.description: Close an existing WebSocket connection. The connection status is updated to 'closed' and all captured messages remain available for retrieval. Parameters: connection_id (string, the WebSocket connection ID to close, required).

connection_id.description: The WebSocket connection ID to close

list.description: List all tracked WebSocket connections, including both programmatically created connections and those intercepted through Burp's proxy. Returns connection summaries with ID, URL, status, and message counts. No parameters required.

get_messages.description: Retrieve messages from a specific WebSocket connection with optional filtering and pagination. Supports cursor-based polling via since_index: pass the index of the last message you read; no frame is ever skipped, and missed_messages counts frames evicted from the buffer (newest 2000 kept) before you read them. The payload of a BINARY frame is base64; length is always the frame size in bytes. To block until a frame arrives use websocket.wait_message instead of polling. Parameters: connection_id (string, required), direction (optional, 'client_to_server', 'server_to_client' or 'both'), since_index (optional integer, only return messages with index greater than this value, default -1 for all), max_results (optional integer, maximum messages to return, default 100).

since_index.description: Only return messages with index greater than this (default -1 for all)

set_intercept_rule.description: Create or update a WebSocket message interception rule. Rules can modify, drop, or tag messages matching specified criteria. Rules are evaluated against all WebSocket traffic passing through Burp, text and binary frames alike: a binary frame is matched and rewritten as ISO-8859-1 text (one character per byte), so \xNN in a regex matches a raw byte and a replacement character U+0000..U+00FF writes one. Parameters: rule_id (optional string, unique ID; auto-generated if not provided), match_url (optional string, regex to match against WebSocket URL), match_message (optional string, regex to match against message content), direction (optional string, 'client_to_server', 'server_to_client', or 'both', default 'both'), action (string, 'modify', 'drop', or 'tag', required), modify_regex (optional string, regex for content replacement when action is 'modify'), modify_replacement (optional string, replacement for regex matches), tag_comment (optional string, comment to attach when action is 'tag'), message_type (optional string, 'TEXT' or 'BINARY' to limit the rule to that kind of frame), enabled (optional boolean, whether the rule is active, default true).

match_url.description: Regex to match against WebSocket URL

match_message.description: Regex to match against message content

modify_regex.description: Regex for content replacement; required when action is 'modify'

tag_comment.description: Comment to attach when action is 'tag'

message_type.description: Limit the rule to 'TEXT' or 'BINARY' frames (case-insensitive); default both

enabled.description: Whether the rule is active (default true)

wait_message.description: Wait for the next WebSocket frame that matches a direction, type and/or regex, instead of polling websocket.get_messages. Blocks until a frame recorded after since_index matches, the connection closes, or timeout_ms passes. Frames already buffered after since_index count: pass the message_index returned by websocket.send_text / websocket.send_binary to get the reply to that message even when it arrived before this call. Without since_index only frames that arrive after the call starts count. Returns {matched: true, message} or {matched: false, reason: 'timeout' | 'connection_closed'}, plus next_since_index to pass as since_index when waiting again. Works on every tracked connection, including those opened through Burp's proxy.

since_index.description: Only frames with an index greater than this count: the message_index of a sent message, or next_since_index of a previous wait; -1 for any retained frame. Default: only frames that arrive after the call starts

direction.description: Direction of the awaited frame (case-insensitive): 'server_to_client' (default), 'client_to_server', or 'both'

message_type.description: Only frames of this type (case-insensitive); default either

pattern.description: Regex (case-insensitive; start it with (?-i) for an exact match) the frame payload must contain; a BINARY frame is matched as ISO-8859-1 text, so \xNN matches a raw byte

timeout_ms.description: How long to wait (default 10000; clamped to 300000; 0 only checks what is already buffered). Keep it below your client's request timeout, often 60000

fuzz.description: Fuzz a WebSocket endpoint: send each payload as one message and get back the frames it triggered, plus clusters of similar responses. Payloads come from 'payloads' and/or a built-in 'payload_library'; with 'template' each payload replaces the marker (default FUZZ) in that message, and payload_encoding 'json' escapes it first for a JSON string. Give connection_id to fuzz over an open connection (one created with websocket.create), or url to open a fresh connection for every payload (for servers that close on bad input); setup_messages are sent first on each connection used. After each payload, server frames are collected until idle_ms pass without a new one (at most window_ms), then delay_ms is waited before the next payload; server frames that arrive before the next payload goes out still count for the previous one. The result lists per payload its frames, response_ms and cluster; 'clusters' groups the payloads whose responses are the same once the echoed payload, timestamps and ids are masked, largest first, so the small clusters are the anomalies. The run stops early (stopped_early, with next_index to pass as start_index) when timeout_ms runs out or the open connection closes. Numbers out of range are clamped and listed under 'clamped'. Scope: advisory only. An out-of-scope target gets scope_warning under mcp_scope_mode warn and enforce; it is never blocked.
